```{r setup}
library(ffp)
```

## What is a view?

Fully Flexible Probabilities represent a distribution through a fixed set of
scenarios and a probability vector. Starting from prior
probabilities \(q_1,\ldots,q_T\), Entropy Pooling searches for posterior
probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_T\) that incorporate new information while
remaining as close as possible to the prior.

A **view** is the way that information is expressed.

<!-- It is useful to distinguish a view from both a forecast and a probability -->
<!-- weight.  -->

A view does not tell `ffp` which scenarios should receive more
probability. Instead, it states a property that the posterior distribution
should satisfy. For example, an investor may believe that expected equity
returns should be 1.5%, that inflation above 4% should occur with probability
10%, or that equity returns should have a higher expected return than bonds 
(positive equity risk premia).

The Entropy Pooling problem can be written generically as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_p
&\quad
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t
\log\left(
\frac{p_t}{q_t}
\right)
\\[4pt]
\text{subject to}
&\quad
A_{\mathrm{eq}}p = b_{\mathrm{eq}},
\\
&\quad
A_{\mathrm{ineq}}p \leq b_{\mathrm{ineq}},
\\
&\quad
p_t \geq 0,
\qquad t=1,\ldots,T,
\\
&\quad
\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_t = 1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The role of the `view_*()` functions is therefore to translate economically
meaningful statements into rows of \(A_{\mathrm{eq}}\),
\(b_{\mathrm{eq}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{ineq}}\), and
\(b_{\mathrm{ineq}}\).

Most users do not need to construct these matrices directly. The view
interface exists precisely so that the analysis can be expressed in terms of
means, probabilities, quantiles, rankings, dispersion, and dependence rather
than low-level constraint matrices.

<!-- One semantic view does not necessarily correspond to one mathematical -->
<!-- constraint. A mean target produces one equality, while a quantile target -->
<!-- requires two inequalities. Ranking several variables or targeting an entire -->
<!-- covariance matrix generates multiple constraints from a single view -->
<!-- specification. -->

This vignette develops these ideas using a common set of simulated scenarios.

## Scenario data

We use 1000 joint scenarios for equity returns, bond returns, and inflation.
The variables are deliberately dependent so that views can act on both
marginal and joint properties of the distribution:

```{r scenarios}
set.seed(123)

n_scenarios <- 1000

growth_shock    <- rnorm(n_scenarios)
inflation_shock <- rnorm(n_scenarios)
market_shock    <- rnorm(n_scenarios)

scenarios <- tibble::tibble(
  equity    = 0.006 + 0.030 * growth_shock - 0.010 * inflation_shock + 0.025 * market_shock,
  bonds     = 0.002 - 0.006 * growth_shock - 0.012 * inflation_shock + 0.008 * market_shock,
  inflation = 0.025 + 0.006 * growth_shock + 0.008 * inflation_shock
)

scenarios
```

We then define the scenario support and assign uniform prior probabilities:

```{r model}
model <- scenarios |>
  ffp_model() |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_uniform()
  )
model
```

Views can only be attached after a prior has been specified. This ordering is
important because some views, particularly those involving second moments,
use reference quantities computed under the current model prior.

## Views on location

### Mean views

A mean view is the most direct example of a linear constraint on scenario
probabilities.

Suppose the posterior expected equity return should be 1.5%:

```{r mean-view}
mean_view <- view_mean(equity, target = 0.015)
mean_view
```

Mathematically, the statement is:

$$
E_p[X]
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_tX_t
=
m,
$$

where \(m\) is the target value. In this example:

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t x_{t,\mathrm{equity}}
=
0.015.
$$

Because the scenario values are fixed, this expression is linear in the
unknown probabilities \(p_t\).

The view can easily then be attached to the model:

```{r attach-mean}
model_mean <- model |>
  ffp_view(mean_view)
model_mean
```

`view_mean()` is not restricted to a single raw column. The `x` argument may
also be an expression evaluated from the scenario data. For example, a view on
the positive equity risk premium of 1% can be written directly as:

```{r mean-expression}
view_mean(equity - bonds, target = 0.01)
```

The expression is evaluated scenario by scenario before the view is compiled,
so the resulting mathematical condition is:

$$
E_p[
\text{equity} - \text{bonds}
]
=
0.01.
$$

Multiple features can also be targeted in one view. In that case, there must
be exactly one target per feature. Targets are matched by position and are not
silently recycled:

```{r mean-panel}
returns <- scenarios |>
  dplyr::select(equity, bonds)

view_mean(returns, target = c(0.015, 0.003))
```

This creates two mean constraints, one for `equity` and one for `bonds`.

### Ranking views

A ranking view is also a statement about posterior means, but it does not
require the user to specify their numerical values. Instead, it imposes an
ordering.

Suppose we believe equity to have a posterior expected return at least as high as
bonds:

```{r rank-view}
view_rank(returns, order = c("equity", "bonds"))
```

For two variables, the view means:

$$
E_p[\text{equity}]
\geq
E_p[\text{bonds}],
$$

which can be rewritten as the linear inequality:

$$
E_p[
\text{bonds} - \text{equity}
]
\leq
0.
$$

More generally, if \(K\) variables are ordered as:

$$
E_p[X_1]
\geq
E_p[X_2]
\geq
\cdots
\geq
E_p[X_K],
$$

`ffp` only needs to impose the adjacent comparisons:

$$
E_p[X_2-X_1] \leq 0,
$$

$$
E_p[X_3-X_2] \leq 0,
$$

and so forth. A ranking of \(K\) features therefore generates
\(K-1\) mathematical inequalities.

The inequalities are weak inequalities. Ties are allowed; `ffp` does not add
an arbitrary epsilon or numerical margin to force strict ordering.

Ranking views are useful when the analyst has a strong relative opinion but
does not want to commit to exact expected-return target. 

## Views on events

### Unconditional probability views

Many economic opinions are naturally expressed as probabilities rather than
moments. Suppose we believe that inflation above 4% should occur with posterior
probability 10%.

```{r probability-view}
view_probability(inflation > 0.04, target = 0.10)
```

The logical expression `inflation > 0.04` creates an indicator for each
scenario. If \(A_t\) equals one when the event occurs and zero otherwise, the
view becomes:

$$
P_p(A)
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t A_t
=
0.10.
$$

The constraint remains linear because the scenario-level event indicators are
known before the optimization begins.

The same interface can express more complex events using ordinary logical
operators. For example:

```{r complex-events}
view_probability(
  equity < 0 & inflation > 0.04,
  target = 0.08
)

view_probability(
  equity < -0.05 | inflation > 0.05,
  target = 0.12
)
```

The first view describes a joint event, whereas the second describes a union of
events. No special probability syntax is required beyond the logical
expressions used in R.

### Conditional probability views

`view_probability()` can also express conditional probabilities through the
`given` argument.

Suppose we define a high-inflation regime and believe that equity losses should
occur with probability 70% conditional on that regime.

```{r conditional-probability}
view_probability(
  equity < 0,
  target = 0.70,
  given  = inflation > 0.035
)
```

For events \(A\) and \(G\), the statement:

$$
P_p(A \mid G)
=
\pi
$$

is equivalent to:

$$
P_p(A \cap G)
-
\pi P_p(G)
=
0.
$$

In scenario form:

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t
\left[
\mathbb{1}(A_t \cap G_t)
-
\pi
\mathbb{1}(G_t)
\right]
=
0.
$$

The ratio implied by conditional probability has therefore been transformed
into a linear equality in the posterior probabilities.

The conditioning event must have positive probability under the current prior.
If the prior assigns zero probability to every scenario in `given`, the
conditional probability is undefined and the view cannot be attached.

## Views on quantiles and medians

### Quantile views

Quantiles require more care because flexible distributions are discrete. The
scenario support is fixed, and `ffp` does not interpolate between scenario
values to create sample quantiles.

Suppose we want \(-6\%\) to be a posterior 5% quantile of equity returns.

```{r quantile-view}
view_quantile(equity, target = -0.06, level = 0.05)
```

For a target \(q\) and quantile level \(u\), the view means that \(q\) belongs
to the set of posterior \(u\)-quantiles. This requires:

$$
P_p(X < q)
\leq
u
$$

and

$$
P_p(X > q)
\leq
1-u.
$$

Equivalently, using the posterior cumulative distribution function:

$$
F_p(q^-)
\leq
u
\leq
F_p(q).
$$

For the example above, `ffp` therefore compiles the two inequalities:

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t
\mathbb{1}
(x_{t,\mathrm{equity}} < -0.06)
\leq
0.05
$$

and

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t
\mathbb{1}
(x_{t,\mathrm{equity}} > -0.06)
\leq
0.95.
$$

This is an important example of the distinction between a **semantic view**
and a **mathematical constraint**. The user expresses one quantile view, but
the compiler needs two inequalities to represent it.

The formulation also handles probability mass located exactly at the target
naturally. No interpolation rule from `stats::quantile()` is involved.

A scalar `level` can be shared across multiple features:

```{r quantile-panel}
view_quantile(
  returns, 
  target = c(-0.06, -0.025), 
  level  = 0.05
)
```

Different features can also use different levels when one level is supplied
for each target:

```{r quantile-mixed-levels}
view_quantile(
  returns,
  target = c(-0.06, 0.03),
  level  = c(0.05, 0.95)
)
```

### Median views

`view_median()` is the median-specific counterpart to `view_quantile()`. It
uses exactly the same discrete-distribution logic with \(u=0.5\).

```{r median-view}
view_median(equity, target = 0.005)
```

The target \(m\) is a posterior median when:

$$
P_p(X < m)
\leq
0.5
$$

and

$$
P_p(X > m)
\leq
0.5.
$$

A median view therefore also generates two inequalities per target. The
dedicated function is mainly a convenience for a common special case of a
quantile view.

## Views on dispersion

Views on variance and volatility introduce an additional idea. A literal
posterior variance:

$$
E_p[X^2] - E_p[X]^2
$$

is nonlinear in the probability vector because the posterior mean itself
depends on \(p\).

The Fully Flexible Views formulation keeps the Entropy Pooling constraints
linear by anchoring the second-moment representation to a **reference mean**
computed under the model prior.

Let:

$$
\hat m_q
=
E_q[X]
$$

denote this prior reference mean.

### Volatility views

For a volatility target \(\sigma^\star\), `view_volatility()` uses:

$$
E_p[X^2]
=
\hat m_q^2
+
(\sigma^\star)^2
$$

In scenario form:

$$
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t X_t^2
=
\hat m_q^2
+
(\sigma^\star)^2
$$

The target is supplied directly in standard-deviation units.

```{r volatility-view}
equity_sd <- stats::sd(scenarios$equity)

view_volatility(
  equity,
  target = equity_sd * 1.10
)
```

The reference mean is not another user parameter. It is calculated internally
from the feature values and the model prior when the view is compiled.

This distinction matters when interpreting the result. The function uses the
linear second-moment representation of a volatility view rather than inserting
the nonlinear expression:

$$
E_p[X^2] - E_p[X]^2
$$

directly into the optimization problem.

### Variance views

`view_variance()` uses the same representation, but its target is expressed in
variance units rather than standard-deviation units.

For variance target \(v^\star\):

$$
E_p[X^2]
=
\hat m_q^2
+
v^\star
$$

For example:

```{r variance-view}
view_variance(
  equity,
  target = equity_sd^2
)
```

The distinction between `view_volatility()` and `view_variance()` is therefore
primarily one of parameterization. The former accepts standard-deviation units,
while the latter accepts squared units.

## Views on dependence

The same linear second-moment approach extends from individual variables to
the dependence structure of several variables.

For the examples below, we work with the two return series:

```{r return-panel}
returns <- scenarios |>
  dplyr::select(equity, bonds)
```

### Covariance views

Suppose \(X_k\) and \(X_l\) are two scenario features and
\(C^\star_{kl}\) is the target covariance between them. Let
\(\hat m_{q,k}\) and \(\hat m_{q,l}\) denote their means under the prior.

The covariance view is represented through

$$
E_p[X_kX_l]
=
\hat m_{q,k}\hat m_{q,l}
+
C^\star_{kl}
$$

For \(K\) features, the user supplies a complete \(K\times K\) target covariance
matrix:

```{r covariance-target}
#shrinkage 
sigma <- stats::cov(returns)
delta <- 0.2 # shrinkage intensity
target_cov <- (1 - delta) * sigma + delta * diag(diag(sigma))
```

The view is then written as

```{r covariance-view}
view_covariance(returns, target = target_cov)
```

Because a covariance matrix is symmetric, `ffp` only needs to compile one
triangular portion. A covariance view on \(K\) features therefore produces:

$$
\frac{K(K+1)}{2}
$$

equality constraints.

The diagonal deserves attention. A complete covariance-matrix view does not
only constrain pairwise covariances; its diagonal also contains variance
targets. In that sense, `view_covariance()` jointly describes marginal
dispersion and cross-variable dependence.

The target must be a valid covariance matrix: numeric, square, finite,
symmetric, and positive semidefinite. When the features and the target matrix
are both named, their order must already agree. `ffp` does not silently reorder
the matrix to match the scenario data.

### Correlation views

Correlation views are represented in a similar way, but they use both prior
reference means and prior reference standard deviations.

Let \(R^\star_{kl}\) denote the desired correlation between features \(k\) and
\(l\). The linear constraint is:

$$
E_p[X_kX_l]
=
\hat m_{q,k}\hat m_{q,l}
+
\hat\sigma_{q,k}
\hat\sigma_{q,l}
R^\star_{kl}
$$

where \(\hat\sigma_{q,k}\) and \(\hat\sigma_{q,l}\) are standard deviations
computed under the model prior.

For two assets, a target correlation matrix might be:

```{r correlation-target}
target_cor <- matrix(
  c(
    1.00, 0.20,
    0.20, 1.00
  ),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    c("equity", "bonds"),
    c("equity", "bonds")
  )
)
target_cor
```

and the corresponding view is:

```{r correlation-view}
view_correlation(returns, target = target_cor)
```

The target must be a valid correlation matrix: it must be symmetric, positive
semidefinite, have unit diagonal, and contain entries between \(-1\) and
\(1\).

A correlation view requires positive reference dispersion for every feature
under the prior. Correlation is undefined when a variable has zero prior
variance.

As with covariance, the full target matrix is meaningful. Since the diagonal
of a valid correlation matrix is one, the diagonal constraints also anchor the
second moments of the individual variables through their prior reference
standard deviations. `view_correlation()` should therefore not be interpreted
as modifying only the off-diagonal entries of a covariance structure.

## Why reference moments are used

The treatment of volatility, variance, covariance and correlation deserves a
short summary because it differs from the direct constraints used for means and
event probabilities.

The key computational requirement of the Entropy Pooling interface is that
views compile into **linear constraints in the posterior probabilities**. Means
and probabilities are already linear in \(p\), but standard deviations,
covariances and correlations would generally become nonlinear if all posterior
moments inside their usual definitions were allowed to move simultaneously.

The Fully Flexible Views formulation avoids this problem by expressing these
views through second moments while keeping selected reference moments fixed
under the prior. The resulting constraints remain linear and can therefore be
combined with the other views in the same Entropy Pooling problem.

This also means that a user should distinguish between a conventional
statistical identity computed entirely under posterior probabilities and the
linear view representation used to obtain those probabilities. Functions such
as `ffp_moments()` can later be used to calculate the actual probability-weighted
posterior moments implied by the fitted distribution.

## Combining views

The real flexibility of the interface appears when several pieces of
information are expressed together.

Consider a modest increase in expected equity returns and a lower probability
of very high inflation:

```{r combined-targets}
equity_target  <- mean(scenarios$equity) + 0.002
high_inflation <- scenarios$inflation > 0.04
inflation_probability_target <- mean(high_inflation) * 0.80

c(
  equity_target = equity_target,
  inflation_probability_target = inflation_probability_target
)
```

We can add both views in one call:

```{r combined-views}
model_views <- model |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = equity_target),
    view_probability(inflation > 0.04, target = inflation_probability_target)
  )
model_views
```

The same model could also have been built incrementally:

```{r combined-incremental}
model_views_incremental <- model |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = equity_target)
  ) |>
  ffp_view(
    view_probability(inflation > 0.04, target = inflation_probability_target)
  )
model_views_incremental
```

The second call does **not** replace the first view. Views accumulate in the
model.

More importantly, fitting the model does not perform one Entropy Pooling update
for the mean view and then use that posterior as a new prior for the probability
view. Instead, all attached views are compiled and solved jointly against the
same original model prior.

The optimization problem is therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_p
&\quad
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t
\log\left(
\frac{p_t}{q_t}
\right)
\\[4pt]
\text{subject to}
&\quad
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t
x_{t,\mathrm{equity}}
=
m^\star,
\\
&\quad
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
p_t
\mathbb{1}
(x_{t,\mathrm{inflation}}>0.04)
=
\pi^\star,
\\
&\quad
p_t \geq 0,
\\
&\quad
\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_t = 1,
\end{aligned}
$$

where \(m^\star\) and \(\pi^\star\) are the two targets supplied above.

We can solve the model as usual:

```{r combined-fit}
fit <- ffp_fit(model_views)
fit
```

This joint treatment is central to interpreting `ffp_view()`. A model with many
views represents one coherent set of statements about a single posterior
distribution.

## Semantic views and mathematical constraints

The examples above show that the number of `view_*()` calls is not necessarily
the number of rows that enter the optimization problem.

A useful summary is:

| View | Mathematical representation |
|---|---|
| `view_mean()` | one equality per target |
| `view_probability()` | one equality per event |
| `view_quantile()` | two inequalities per target |
| `view_median()` | two inequalities per target |
| `view_rank()` | \(K-1\) inequalities for \(K\) ranked features |
| `view_volatility()` | one second-moment equality per target |
| `view_variance()` | one second-moment equality per target |
| `view_covariance()` | \(K(K+1)/2\) equalities |
| `view_correlation()` | \(K(K+1)/2\) equalities |

The user-facing API is deliberately semantic: it records what the analyst means.
The compiler handles the mathematical expansion needed by Entropy Pooling.

This separation is especially useful for quantiles and matrix views, where
writing the corresponding constraint matrices manually would quickly become
cumbersome and error-prone.

## Scenario support and feasibility

A view can only redistribute probability over scenarios that already exist in
the model. This creates an important relationship between the scenario support
and the views that can be imposed.

For example, a posterior mean must lie inside the convex hull of the available
scenario values. If every equity return in the support is below 5%, then a
full-confidence view requiring an expected return of 10% cannot be satisfied
simply by changing probabilities.

Similarly, if no scenario satisfies an event, its posterior probability can
only be zero. Entropy Pooling cannot assign positive probability to an outcome
that does not exist in the support.

Quantile views are also constrained by the available scenario values and
probability mass, while combinations of individually reasonable views may still
be mutually inconsistent.

This limitation is not a defect of Entropy Pooling. It is a direct consequence
of the modeling principle that the scenarios remain fixed while only their
probabilities change.

For this reason, scenario design becomes especially important when working with
extreme views or stress scenarios. If an economically relevant state of the
world is absent from the support, probability reweighting alone cannot create
it.

A feasible solution may also lie on the boundary of the probability simplex,
meaning that some posterior scenario probabilities are exactly zero. Such a
boundary solution is not automatically a numerical failure; it may be the
correct full-confidence solution implied by the views.

Detailed numerical assessment of the fitted problem belongs to
`ffp_diagnostics()`.

## Full confidence and partial confidence

Every view attached to a model and passed to `ffp_fit()` is treated with
**full confidence**. The posterior probabilities are chosen so that the compiled
view constraints are satisfied, subject to numerical precision.

This is different from saying that the analyst is completely certain about the
economic opinion itself.

When views should influence the distribution without being imposed with full
confidence, `ffp_opinion_pooling()` provides a separate step after fitting. If
\(p_{\mathrm{full}}\) is the full-confidence posterior and \(c\) is a global
confidence level, the partially confident distribution is:

$$
p_c
=
(1-c)q
+
c p_{\mathrm{full}}
$$

For example:

```{r partial-confidence}
pooled <- ffp_opinion_pooling(fit, confidence = 0.75)
pooled
```

The distinction between these layers is important. `view_*()` specifies what
the posterior should say. `ffp_fit()` solves that problem under full
confidence. `ffp_opinion_pooling()` subsequently expresses how strongly the
analyst believes the collection of views.

<!-- View confidence must also be distinguished from numerical solver tolerances. -->
<!-- Confidence is an economic modeling choice, whereas tolerances determine how -->
<!-- numerical constraint satisfaction is assessed. -->

## A compact view workflow

Once the meaning of the individual view types is understood, a relatively rich
model can still be expressed compactly.

```{r compact-workflow, eval = FALSE}
fit <- scenarios |>
  ffp_model() |>
  ffp_prior(
    prior_uniform()
  ) |>
  ffp_view(
    view_mean(equity, target = 0.015),
    view_probability(inflation > 0.04, target = 0.10),
    view_rank(returns, order = c("equity", "bonds"))
  ) |>
  ffp_fit()
```

<!-- Despite the compact syntax, the economic meaning remains explicit: one view -->
<!-- targets an expected return, another targets the probability of an inflation -->
<!-- event, and another imposes a relative ordering of expected asset returns. -->
<!-- `ffp` compiles these statements into their corresponding equality and -->
<!-- inequality constraints and solves them jointly in a single Entropy Pooling -->
<!-- problem. -->

The purpose of the view interface is therefore not merely to shorten code. It
creates a separation between the analyst's economic statements and the
numerical representation required to enforce them.

## Where to go next

Views are only one component of a Fully Flexible Probabilities model. The prior
determines how scenario probabilities are distributed before subjective
information is introduced, while the views describe the properties that the
full-confidence posterior should satisfy.

After fitting, `ffp_stats()`, `ffp_risk()`, and `ffp_moments()` can be used to
study the economic consequences of the probability update.
`ffp_diagnostics()` provides the complementary numerical perspective by showing
how the compiled constraints behave and whether the Entropy Pooling problem is
regular, on the boundary, or infeasible.

When views are economically uncertain, `ffp_opinion_pooling()` keeps that
question separate from both view specification and numerical solution. This
separation between **prior information**, **view content**, **numerical
feasibility**, and **view confidence** is one of the central organizing ideas
of the `ffp` 2.0 workflow.
